text:
United Nations Development Assistance Framework
for Ukraine
Prepared by
The United Nations Country Team in Ukraine
December, 2001
(Draft 18 December 2001)
Table of Contents
I.	Executive Summary	2
II.	Rationale for the UNDAF	3
III. Goals and Objectives	5
IV. UN System Cooperation Strategies	11
V.  	Follow Up and Review	24
VI.  UNDAF Programme Resources 2002-2005 (US$ Millions)	27
Executive Summary
Since its independence in 1991, Ukraine has gone through a dramatic transition.  The establishment of a market economy and the growth of personal freedoms have fundamentally changed the face of the country and its future direction.  Endowed with highly educated people and a wealth of natural resources, Ukraine is showing signs of realizing its potential for high economic growth and prosperity.  On the other hand, the transition has not been smooth nor easy.  The political and economic reform process is incomplete and the wellbeing of the people, measured by indicators of human development, has declined and many people are living in poverty.  
The present circumstances present a dual opportunity for the UN family. First, to support the achievement of the vision of Ukraine as a functioning democracy, respectful of human rights and with a job creating, market economy that is globally competitive. Second to address the needs of vulnerable groups who have been adversely affected by the transition.  
Guided by national goals, global commitments of the Government, and analysis undertaken in the UN Common Country Assessment (CCA), the United Nations Development Assistance Framework for Ukraine (UNDAF) focuses on priority areas for assistance that will emphasize:
the promotion of economic growth with equity as the engine for improving the standard of living of the people and overcoming poverty;
better access to and quality of social services to build, maintain and care for the country’s human capital, including the most vulnerable;
sustainable use of the nation’s natural wealth for the present and future generations;
improvement of governance institutions and practices to give primacy to planning and implementation for human development;
reaching the national goals that have been set on HIV/AIDS to reduce the rate of infection and to provide care and compassion to those who have been infected and affected .
The UN system recognizes that Ukraine’s human capital, history and culture, and natural resources can be powerful springboards for development.  The strategy of the UN system will be to concentrate its efforts on adapting human capacities of the country to meet the needs of a modern economy and on further development of institutions that govern and provide services to efficiently meet the needs of the people.
The UNDAF represents the blueprint that has been agreed with the Ukraine Government for UN support to Ukraine in the coming years. Individual UN Agencies will use the UNDAF as the broad basis for their subsequent programming exercises.  The United Nations Country Team (UNCT) in Ukraine is grateful to the many people and organizations that have contributed to both the CCA and the UNDAF. The UNCT hopes to continue this partnership forward into design and implementation stages to support Ukraine in reaching its many national goals, including those that were set at the Millennium Summit. 
Rationale for the UNDAF
Major Issues Facing Ukraine.  Though in the near term Ukraine’s economic picture is improving, the results of the ten years of decline have significantly undermined living standards.  Over 25% of the population now lives below the official poverty line.  Major social services in health, education and social welfare have deteriorated.  Reforms in these areas are constrained by lack of funds and resistance to change from vested interests.  Alternative forms of service delivery are emerging in civil society organizations and the private sector.   The transition from top-down to democratic governance is moving forward in some areas, particularly in increased citizen participation in decision-making, the expanding role of civil society organizations, and decentralization of authority to local government.  However, the implementation of governance reforms lags well behind the passage of related laws and policies.  The environment, still reeling from the effects of the Chernobyl disaster 15 years ago, suffers the effects of severe pollution from heavy industry, mining, and the burning of fossil fuels.  Deforestation in western Ukraine has caused flooding, erosion and loss of bio-diversity.  Finally, the new plague of HIV/AIDS infection has taken hold in Ukraine and is rapidly expanding.  The Government is moving boldly to address HIV/AIDS, but the public health and related services remain unprepared to deal with the epidemic.
Rationale for UN Development Assistance.  Ukraine is a founding member of the United Nations and has been increasingly active in UN affairs since independence. Ukraine has also established cooperation agreements with many specialized agencies of the UN system. The first representative of the UN system arrived in Ukraine in 1992.  Since then, several UN agencies have established offices or representation arrangements in the country and have begun to carry out programme activities.  The UN Development Assistance Framework, the first for this country, has been prepared in the context of this active and growing partnership between Ukraine and the UN system.  
Development assistance from the UN system to Ukraine is based first and foremost on national priorities, strategies, programmes articulated by the Government and on the commitments of the State to the achievement of the Millenium Summit goals.  Second, UN assistance to Ukraine is based on the competence and comparative advantages of UN agencies to make strategically important interventions.  The members of the UN Country Team limited the coverage of the Common Country Assessment to five areas in which UN agencies have global mandates and national experience in Ukraine.  In all of these five areas - poverty, social services, governance, environment and HIV/AIDS - the technical expertise of UN agencies has been making and can continue to make strategic contributions to Ukraine. 
Third, though the UN system has limited resources, on the basis of the global and national experience and expertise of UN agencies, the UN system is strategically placed to leverage its core resources through partnerships with other development partners.  
Fourth, within the thematic areas, the issues are complex and inter-related.  The UNDAF will seek to outline, to the greatest extent possible, the comprehensive and coordinated response from the UN system that the issues demand. 
Finally, the UN system will provide support to Ukraine under the UNDAF for monitoring and implementation of activities for fulfillment of its commitments on national development made at the Millenium Summit. 
III. Goals and Objectives
Goals.  The goals of the Government in the five thematic areas identified in the Common Country Assessment are expressed in national policies and programmes and Millenium Summit Development Goals.  These goals are fully supported by the UN system.  The goals seek to achieve the following results in the mid to long term:
Poverty Reduction:  A significant reduction of poverty in Ukraine by 2015
Social Services:  High quality services in health, education and social welfare that are provided effectively and equitably to meet the needs of the general population, children, and other vulnerable groups;  Meeting Millenium Summit targets for reduction in maternal mortality and access to and completion of primary education
Governance:  Governance that is effective and accountable at both the national and local levels based on rule of law, respect for human rights and the will of the people
Environment: Sustainable use of natural resources for economic growth, protection of the people from the harmful effects of pollution, preservation of unique natural resources.
HIV/AIDS:  Effective prevention of HIV/AIDS and reduction of the harmful effects of the disease on society
Objectives of Assistance from the UN System.  The UN system has set out objectives for its assistance to support each goal of the Government.  The achievement of each objective will require interventions in a number of areas from the UN system and other development partners.  UN agencies must approve funding or mobilize other resources for many of the interventions identified in the UNDAF. 
For each objective, the areas for operational activities are listed along with generic indicators for measurement of performance. The concerned UN agencies will determine the actual indicators to be used in these areas during their programming processes and will be accountable for monitoring and evaluation of the programme activities that they fund.   The objective for goal #5 has been expanded to include UN system responses in other areas that require multi-sectoral approaches, namely, Chernobyl and re-integration of formerly deported persons in the Crimea.
Objective 1. Poverty Reduction through Economic Growth and Job Creation.  The UN system will provide advice to the Government and strengthen its capacity to develop and implement appropriate policies and programmes for sustainable, equitable economic growth and stability, further reform of the economy, and the promotion of trade and investment.  The UN system will promote and strengthen capacities for job creation, access to financial and information resources and development of skills in private and civil society organizations.  Table 1 below indicates areas of UN system activity under this objective and possible types of indicators to measure performance.
Objective 2. Improved Social Services To Improve Quality of Life and Reduce Poverty. The UN system will advise the Government and strengthen its capacity to develop, sustain and implement appropriate policies and quality programmes for equitable access to and reform of the education and health systems.  The UN system will also support the provision of targeted services for vulnerable groups, including refugees, asylum seekers and children in need of special protection in accordance with international standards.  The UN system will strengthen the capacity of relevant civil society organizations to provide services to vulnerable groups and will support policy development on human development and poverty and related capacity building for data collection, review and analysis. The UN system will provide direct support to asylum seekers, victims of emergencies, and communities receiving formerly deported persons.
Objective 3. Governance: The UN system will strengthen the capacity of Government and will build partnerships with civil society organizations to enhance citizen participation in decision making about public policies and programmes.  The UN system will also advise the Government and strengthen its capacity to develop and implement appropriate policies and programmes for public sector reform, transparency and accountability in government, decentralization, and strengthening of local government. The UN system will promote greater awareness of and respect for human rights. 
Objective 4.  Environment.  The UN System will advise the Government and strengthen its capacity to implement appropriate policies and programmes on sustainable development and use of natural resources, energy efficiency, soil and water pollution, climate change, pollution of international waters, and bio-diversity.  The UN system will promote public awareness of environmental issues, public participation in decision-making to resolve those issues, and local level environmental management.
Objective 5.  HIV/AIDS and Other Multi-Sectoral Activities.  The UN System will advise the Government on HIV/AIDS policies, provide direct technical support to the Government on HIV/AIDS issues, and strengthen national capacities to develop and implement appropriate policies and programmes on HIV prevention, surveillance, counseling and testing, care for people who are infected, and medical treatment.  The UN system will promote partnerships with other international organizations and national civil society organizations to address HIV/AIDS.  The UN system will advise the Government on appropriate policies and strengthen national capacities to implement appropriate programmes in areas of high priority that require multi-sectoral responses.
IV. UN System Cooperation Strategies
The UN system cooperation strategies are based on national strategies and programmes, the needs identified in the Common Country Assessment, and the Millenium Summit Goals.  UN agencies cooperate among themselves and with Bretton Woods institutions on the basis of mutual agreement and in accordance with their mandates and comparative advantages on particular activities.  Inter-agency cooperation may occur in many forms and at varying levels of intensity.  These methods of cooperation include: joint activities in which all participating agencies jointly plan and implement programme activities; coordinated activities that are organized on the basis of inter-agency consultation on agency-specific activities to meet common goals; and complementary activities that are agency-specific but on different subjects within the same sector or area.  Finally, UN agencies need not cooperate in every area.  They may carry out independent activities, unilateral agency-specific activities in accordance with their unique mandates.
The UN Country Team facilitates inter-agency cooperation by carrying out system-wide advocacy, establishing working groups to explore and develop collaborative approaches, fostering joint programming and coordinated programming, information sharing among agencies, and encouraging the establishment of strategic partnerships with other development partners and civil society organizations.
The cooperation and operational strategies of the UN system and Bretton Woods institutions are presented below for each objective of the UNDAF.  An overview table is presented for each objective that lists the areas of intervention, the UN agencies that are providing assistance in that area, and other development agencies that are also active in the area. In general, operational strategies of individual UN agencies include advocacy; analytical work and policy dialogue; pilot projects; the creation, development or transformation of institutional capacities; development and balance of payments loans; direct investments, and in some cases, direct support for the provision of essential services. The presentation of cooperation strategies below illustrates that there are many remaining opportunities for additional collaboration and synergies among the activities of the UN agencies and the Bretton Woods institutions.
Cooperation Strategy for Objective 1:   
Poverty Reduction through Economic Growth and Job Creation
The cooperation strategy for poverty reduction through economic growth and job creation focuses on basic causes of poverty resulting from both deficiencies in macro-economic policies and constraints on opportunities for individuals.  The Bretton Woods institutions are the key players in the implementation of this strategy.  The strategy focuses on the need for clear and consistent macro-economic policies that promote growth, stability, and the continuing transition to the market economy.  The strategy also focuses on continuing reforms for private sector and agricultural development.  In order to ensure equitable growth, the strategy also addresses job creation and access to resources at the level of small and medium scale enterprises and individuals.  Table 6 provides an overview of ongoing and planned assistance from the UN system and the Bretton Woods institutions in this area. 
Macro-economic, fiscal and monetary policies for growth and stability.  The IMF and the World Bank spearhead assistance in this area working in close cooperation. The IMF is the main provider of advice to the Government on macro-economic, fiscal, and monetary policies. Both the IMF and the World Bank undertake macro-economic and sectoral analytical work to provide the basis for policy recommendations.  The implementation of policy recommendations is a condition for receipt of loan proceeds from both international financial institutions. The IMF has an Extended Fund Facility (EFF) of $2.6 billion in place for 1999-2002 which was recently re-activated following submission by the Government of its budget for 2002 to the Parliament.  World Bank lending is also linked to structural reforms.  The World Bank plans to  disburse a $750 million Program Adjustment Loan (PAL) in three installments conditioned on performance in achieving reforms in public sector accountability, the regulatory framework for business, property rights and improvements in the delivery of social services.  Both the IMF and the World Bank will be reviewing their lending strategies in 2003.
The World Bank and UNDP are also taking into account potential adverse effects of macro-economic and fiscal policies on the poor.  UNDP is planning to study the effects of economic reform and tax policies on the poor, the unemployed and other vulnerable groups.  The World Bank is supporting efforts to reform the pension system and is also providing loan funds to mitigate the social consequences of closure of 50 uneconomic coal mines including ensuring payments of wage arrears and severance and retraining miners for other occupations.
Privatization and Private Sector Development.  The World Bank and its private sector arm, the International Finance Corporation (IFC), are taking a coordinated approach in their assistance for privatization and private sector development.  In general, the World Bank focuses on the enabling environment for privatization and private sector development and IFC on micro-economic interventions. World Bank lending supports and leverages changes in the regulatory environment for business, promotion of direct foreign investment, access to credit, access to markets and property rights. In regard to the latter, the Title Registration and Distribution operation is a critical building block for the development of the market economy and for the protection of property rights.  The implementation of this project is a precondition for the successful transfer of state assets to private firms or individuals.  
Since 1992, the IFC has been a key player in Ukraine’s transition from a centrally-planned to a market economy.  IFC has completed a number of initiatives in small and large business privatization, development of local consulting capacity, and improvement of the regulatory environment for small and medium scale industries. IFC currently has ongoing and planned programmes on upgrading business and management skills of Ukrainian enterprise through improved corporate governance, financial and asset management, and improving access to business and market information.  IFC will also continue efforts to improve the business and foreign investment climate in Ukraine and will support local financial institutions and the development of the leasing industry to improve private sector access to financing. IFC has approved direct investments totaling $30 million in financial institutions in Ukraine and plans to expand direct investments in other sectors of the economy.
UNDP has parallel programmes supporting SME development that include SME centers to provide advice and training to businesses and to facilitate their access to commercially available credit.  UNDP will also support the establishment of a business incubator for young companies. 
UNIDO will continue to support an initiative for the facilitation of technical information exchange and business cooperation between Ukrainian and firms and research institutions and foreign partners.  UNIDO is also planning a project to strengthen capacities in Ukrainian food processing industries.
Agricultural Development and Land Reform.  The World Bank, IFC and UNDP are the lead agencies in promotion of agricultural development and related reform. The aforementioned World Bank project on property rights is a key element of agricultural reform as it involves the privatization of collective farm land, assets and business activities.  IFC has been active with other donors in developing models for the break up of collective farms and in providing technical assistance to new agro-businesses, concentrating on supply chain development and building linkages between suppliers, processors, financiers and consumers.  UNDP will support policy development for agricultural reform with analytical work on alternative models for reform. 
Job Creation and Access to Resources.  IFC, ILO and UNDP have or are planning activities to promote job creation and access to resources. UNDP is promoting policy reform that will encourage greater labor mobility that should increase access to job opportunities and resources.  IFC has made direct investments in a micro-finance bank in collaboration with EBRD that has made over 600 loans since January 2001.  Based on its SME project, UNDP plans to start a more broadly based approach as an element of its poverty alleviation strategy, targeting rural areas where poverty is a serious problem.  This approach will promote access to many types of resources: financial assets, information technology, vocational training and training in entrepreneurship.  Women and youth will be encouraged to participate in this project.  ILO will continue to support ongoing capacity building activities at the National Vocational Training Center.  
Opportunities for Expanded Cooperation.  There are opportunities for greater cooperation in a number of areas.  IFC and UNDP should be able to share experience and possibly increase cooperation in the areas of SME development, agricultural development, and micro-finance and other financing instruments.  UNDP and ILO should be able to coordinate planned activities for vocational training with micro-finance activities.
Cooperation Strategy for Objective 2: 
Improved Social Services To Reduce Poverty and Improve Quality of Life
The cooperation strategy for improved social services to reduce poverty and improve quality of life seeks to increase access to, sustain and improve the quality of social services.  Such improvements will be of primary benefit to the poor who do not have access to social services, but UN system activities will also benefit the general public.  The UN agencies with mandates and programmes in the social sectors are the key agencies for the implementation of this cooperation strategy, namely, UNICEF, UNFPA, UNHCR, WHO and UNDP.  The strategy emphasizes reform, maintenance and capacity development of social service delivery systems, participation of civil society organizations, and support for policy development for human development and poverty alleviation.  Table 7 provides an overview of ongoing and planned assistance from the UN system and the Bretton Woods institutions in this area.
Access to, Reform of and Capacity Building for the Education System.  The UN Country Team has established a working group to determine ways and means of increasing collaboration among member agencies working in the education sector (WB, UNDP, UNICEF).  All three agencies are planning new multi-year activities.   
Currently, the World Bank, UNDP and UNICEF are supporting the development of education reform strategies with high emphasis on citizen participation. The World Bank is emphasizing the need for developing new ways of financing education. UNDP is supporting the dissemination of the results of studies on education reform and along with UNICEF is promoting national debate on education policy, based on the right of all children to high quality education.  On the basis on the new policy framework, UNDP plans to support the implementation of high priorities in education reform.  UNDP is also continuing a curriculum reform and textbook revision project for primary and secondary education.  UNICEF is exploring the possibilities to support Government efforts to revise standards for primary and secondary education and to conduct pilot activities that integrate child rights and the promotion of healthy life-styles, including reproductive health into school curricula.  At the tertiary level, the World Bank is working on the development of a State loan fund for students in higher education and UNDP has been promoting the use of information technology to increase to knowledge and develop the capacities of university libraries.
UNDP is also planning to implement a multi-faceted project for the promotion of information and communications technology.  Major activities of this project support in school and continuing education, including the development of a network based distance learning platform to be shared by a number of educational institutions; an innovation center to link university researchers and students with business incubators;  an national research and education network linking academic and research institutions; and a model United Nations for youth to learn about and debate technology issues confronting Ukraine.
Access to, Reform of and Capacity Building for the Health System.  WHO and the World Bank are both assisting the Government in health policy development and strategies for health care reform.  The World Bank places particular emphasis on obtaining citizen input into the design of the health care reform strategy and stresses the need for new ways of financing and delivering health care.  WHO focuses on regulation of pharmaceuticals, improving the quality of primary health care, strengthening family health services, improving the health information system, and reform of nursing education.
WHO, UNFPA, UNDP and UNICEF are all supporting improvements in the provision of health services.  WHO is strengthening capacity in the health system for control of tuberculosis; UNFPA is strengthening capacity to deliver reproductive health services and UNICEF is supporting several programmes to improve the health and development of young children, especially through breastfeeding, the promotion of universal iodization of salt, and expanded vaccination programmes.  UNICEF is also supporting “youth friendly” health services through partnerships with local governments and non-governmental organizations.  UNICEF is also involved together with UNFPA, in supporting peer to peer education related to adolescent drug abuse and sexually transmitted diseases.  UNDP’s information and communication technology project includes a component on tele-medicine, a secure network linking Ukraine’s hospital, clinics, and doctors for sharing medical data, imagery, and diagnostic tools over the Internet.
(Note:  Health activities related to HIV/AIDS are presented in the cooperation strategy for objective #5 below.)
Access to, Reform of and Capacity Building for Social Services.  ILO, UNHCR, and UNICEF all are providing or plan to provide assistance targeted at various groups in Ukraine. (UNDP and UNFPA assistance for social services will be discussed in the cooperation strategy for objective #5.)  The groups targeted for UN system assistance are children in need of special protection, refugees and asylum seekers, and the disabled.
UNICEF’s child protection programmes are aimed at three groups of children in need of special care: children deprived of parental care, especially those in state institutions, street children and disabled children.  UNICEF will seek to improve the legal and regulatory framework on child protection and the provision of social services for these children; to transform and develop the state system of care for children with special needs;  to promote and pilot new approaches, such as day care for disabled children and foster families for children currently institutionalized; to research the situation of street children and to support efforts of state agencies, churches and civil society organizations that are providing shelter and services for street children.  
ILO will continue to implement its programme entitled “Elimination of the Worst Forms of Child Labor in Ukraine” in collaboration with Government agencies, non-government organizations, unions and employers.  In addition, ILO is proposing to implement a large project to support the National Center for the Vocational Rehabilitation of the Disabled.  The project, which would support the development of the system for vocational rehabilitation of the disabled in Ukraine, is seeking donor funding.  
UNHCR will place emphasis on developing the capacity of the state agencies to implement new laws on refugees and asylum matters in order to regularise processes for persons in need of international protection.  UNHCR will also continue to advocate for Ukraine's accession to the 1951 Convention on Refugees and its 1967 Protocol, and 1954 Convention on Statelessness.  In order to deal with the regional dimensions of refugee movement and migration, UNHCR will work closer with its offices in neighboring countries to promote cross-border cooperation on migration management including regular information sharing.  UNHCR will continue to assist the Government by promoting local integration through the creation of socio-economic opportunities and self-reliance programmes, and provision of basic needs of most vulnerable refugees and other persons of concern. 
Policy Development on Human Development and Poverty and Related Capacity Building for Data Analysis.  UNDP, the World Bank and ILO are all working on data collection, review and analysis to support policy development in the areas of human development and poverty alleviation.
UNDP is continuing with its series of National Human Development Reports (NHDRs) to provide basic data and neutral analyses to support national policy development on poverty alleviation and other human development issues.  The reports provide standardized summaries of human development status on a number of globally comparable indicators. The coming issues of NHDRs will feature thematic treatment of linkages between governance reforms and human development.  The preparation of the NHDRs will involve many state agencies, academia and the media and will include capacity building activities with these partners on data collection, analysis, public discussion and review, and dissemination of findings.
To continue its support for the conceptualization and implementation of the Government’s Poverty Reduction Strategy, the World Bank will provide technical assistance to support the development of an improved methodology for measurement of poverty, the determination of the minimum level for subsistence and introducing the system for monitoring of the quality of life in Ukraine
ILO plans to continue its related work in the development of socio-economic security indicators for workers in Ukraine and to carry out the second round of a socio-economic survey of 33,000 households for comparison with a similar survey done in 2000.  ILO will also continue to support the development of a budgeting model for social services and benefits with the Ministry of Labor.  A social expenditure survey is also planned.
In the context of the preparation of its next cooperation programme, UNICEF will undertake analyses of the various aspects of the situation of children in Ukraine.
Opportunities for Expanded Cooperation.  Given the extent of interest in the UN system on poverty alleviation, theme group might be established comprised of members of all agencies working on poverty alleviation.  There would appear to opportunity for closer cooperation among the World Bank, UNDP and ILO on policy development and basic data on poverty alleviation and human development.  
Cooperation Strategy for Objective 3: Improved Governance
The cooperation strategy for governance places primary emphasis on increasing citizen participation in governance processes, reform of public sector institutions,  increasing accountability and transparency in government, and decentralization and strengthening of local government.  The strategy will also support the Government in meeting its obligations under international human right conventions and the bringing the national legal framework in the harmony of European laws and regulations.  The World Bank and UNDP are the lead UN agencies in governance.  Table 8 provides an overview of ongoing and planned assistance from the UN system and the Bretton Woods institutions in this area.
Participatory Policy Development. UNDP has ongoing and planned activities supporting the participation of citizens and civil society organizations in policy formulation and implementation and the dissemination of information to the public using modern information technology.  The UNDP-funded information and communications technology project will establish a civil society Internet portal to give Ukrainian NGOs a cost-effective voice on the Internet.  UNDP will also support national academic institutions and non-governmental organizations to carry out research and analysis of the Government’s policies and programmes. These institutions will also hold public forums to discuss policy initiatives and their research findings in order to strengthen the processes of dialogue and consensus building.  As noted in the discussion of social services, UNDP is supporting a participatory process on the development of a national strategy for education reform.  
The participation of young people in the design and implementation of activities intended from them is a key strategy for UNICEF.  UNICEF relies on partnerships with civil society organizations for both programme development and implementation and for advocacy on behalf of children and young people. Youth information centers enable young people to get the knowledge they need to make their participation informed and relevant.  UNICEF will use the findings of a recent youth opinion poll in the design of future youth programmes. 
The World Bank though its ongoing “People’s Voice” Project and related activities is seeking to improve accountability at the municipal level.  The project seeks to  strengthen the capacity of civil society to articulate and disseminate the views and needs of the people regarding improvements in local government and the provision of social services.  Currently in the pilot phase, the project surveys citizens, business leaders and Government officials in a sample of municipalities regarding problems in the delivery of public services.  Results of the surveys are widely disseminated through mass media, public discussions, and civil society organizations.  The project also provides technical assistance to municipalities that wish to increase their responsiveness in service provision.  
Public Sector Reform.  The World Bank has a number of ongoing initiatives including the provision of advice on national fiscal policies on taxation and inter-governmental finance and strengthening institutional capacities in tax administration, budget management, financial management, civil service reform.  UNDP is focusing on strategy development, reform and capacity building for financial audit.
Decentralization and Strengthening of Local Government.  The demand creation side of the World Bank’s strategy for improvement of local government was described above in the section on Participatory Policy Development.  The supply side of the strategy consists of two financial facilities, the Municipal Development Fund and the Social Investment Fund.  The former aims to strengthen local government capacities for financial management and service delivery.  The latter offers targeted financial assistance to poorer communities.   
UNDP will support the development of enabling legislation that will further devolve authority to regional and local levels, strengthening of local government capacities, pilot projects for best practices in local government, and the promotion of local partnerships among government, the private sector and civil society organizations.
UNICEF currently has partnership agreements for a range of social service activities with four municipalities and plans to extend the scale and scope of these agreements.
Gender Issues. UNDP has developed a strategy on promoting gender equality in Ukraine for 2001-2005. The UNDP gender programme will work with state institutions, civil society, other UN agencies and other donor organizations to implement projects in the strategy aiming to provide specific support to and coordination between stakeholders. Specific projects identified in the strategy include gender monitoring of legislation, support for partnership of male and female politicians, gender education in the school system, equal access to information technology, new gender roles for men, and gender sensitive business centers.  These projects will support advocacy for greater participation of women in decision-making roles in Parliament, the cabinet and the civil service, women’s entrepreneurship including greater access to financial assets and technology and the personal security of women and their needs for protection from violence. 
The World Bank will complete and follow up on a study in progress of the effects of the transition on gender issues with particular emphasis on access to finance.  The study will also identify policy options for consideration.  IFC integrates gender considerations into all of its programme activities.  
Human Rights and Access to Legal Aid.  The Resident Coordinator and concerned agencies of the UN system will work with the relevant Government agencies to develop a human rights plan of action pursuant to Government accession to global human rights covenants.  The concerned agencies will also work with the Government to implement the plan and to support public awareness on human rights issues.
UNDP will support expanded access to legal aid clinics to assist those who are poor, ill, or otherwise disadvantaged to enable them to secure their full legal rights and protections.  UNDP will also support the establishment of pilot regional public advocate offices.
UNHCR will continue to advocate for accession to the 1951 Convention on Refugees with the Government and for effective implementation of new Ukrainian laws on citizenship, immigration and child protection and other human rights conventions affecting refugees.  
UNICEF will continue its efforts to make the Convention on the Rights of the Child known, understood, and respected at all levels of society, and to promote effective monitoring of the implementation of the Convention in accordance with the Government’s obligations.
ILO has begun a large project promoting workers’ rights based on eight ILO conventions, all of which have been ratified by the Government.  The rights and principles in these conventions include free association, collective bargaining, non-discrimination in the employment, education and training, and elimination of forced and child labor.  The project will include studies of the labor market, training for union and NGO personnel, training for state labor inspectors, public information activities, and advice on revision of labor laws and assistance in the preparation of a new labor code.
Opportunities for Expanded Cooperation.  There would appear to be opportunities for information sharing and possibly greater collaboration between UNDP and the World Bank in the areas of citizen participation in local governance and other strategies for improving local government.  Some collaboration on gender issues may also be possible.
Cooperation Strategy for Objective 4:  Environmental Management
The cooperation strategy of the UN system emphasizes improvements in the legal and regulatory frameworks for environmental management, strengthening national and local capacities for environmental management, addressing regional environmental issues, implementing global commitments, and eliminating the dangerous source of toxic waste that exists in the stockpile of out of date land mines.  UNDP and the World Bank are the lead agencies in environmental management.  Table 9 provides an overview of ongoing and planned assistance from the UN system and the Bretton Woods institutions in this area.
Legal, Regulatory and Policy Frameworks.  The World Bank is providing assistance for the further development of the legal and regulatory frameworks for environmental management.  UNDP is supporting Government efforts to comply with commitments agreed at the Rio de Janeiro Conference on the Environment and Development and preparation for the European Ministerial Meeting, “Kiev 2002”, which will seek consensus on European environmental policies. In accordance with the global agreement on climate change, the Bank and UNDP will assist the Government to limit greenhouse gas emissions in Ukraine.
Environmental Management Capacity.  Both the World Bank and UNDP are supporting the development of national institutional capacities for policy making and environmental management. UNDP will support integration of environmental management issues into local governance.  The Bank will begin preparations with the Government for environmental investment projects for reduction of air pollution, and improvements in the management of air quality, land resources, and solid wastes. UNDP will support interventions to preserve Ukraine’s biodiversity in arid, semi-arid and forest ecosystems.  UNIDO has proposed to set up a “clean production center” in Ukraine to demonstrate cleaner production technologies for various industrial sectors.
Energy Efficiency.  UNDP is planning to implement a large project with funding from the Global Environmental Facility to promote energy efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The project will establish a pilot private energy service company at the municipal level based on energy efficient technology and will promote public awareness of energy efficiency issues. The World Bank will complete a project on the installation of an efficient de-centralized gas-fired district heating system in Sevastopol. IAEA will continue to provide support for maintaining the safety of nuclear power facilities in the country. 
Regional Activities.  UNDP will provide assistance on a regional basis (including Russia, Belarus and Moldova) for pollution reduction of international waters, namely, the Dnieper and Danube Rivers and the Black Sea.  The regional activities will include a Strategic Action Plan for the Dneiper and pollution reduction projects for the Danube and the Black Sea.  The World Bank will address coastal zone management issues along the Black Sea coast.  
Land Mines.  UNDP will undertake development of a methodology for the safe disposal of Ukraine’s large stockpile of PFM land mines.  The shelf life of these land mines has expired and they are in danger of leaking and spontaneous detonation.  The mines contain toxic substances and are potentially a large environmental hazard.  UNDP will also undertake resource mobilization to carry out actual disposal of the stockpile.
Opportunities for Expanded Cooperation.  There would appear to be scope for additional collaboration between UNDP and the World Bank in regard to the measures being taken to control pollution of international waters.  In the Black Sea, UNDP is working on pollution reduction and the Bank on coastal zone management.  In regard to pollution of the Dneiper River, UNDP regional activities need to take into account national activities for the abatement of pollution by radioactive water being undertaken under the continuing response to Chernobyl.  (See Cooperation Strategy for Objective #5 below.)
Cooperation Strategy for Objective 5:
Addressing HIV/AIDS and Other Multi-Sectoral Issues
The cooperation strategy for this objective addresses three large multi-sectoral problems in Ukraine: HIV/AIDS, Chernobyl and Crimean Re-integration.  In each area, the UN system will continue to mobilize multi-agency responses to the extent possible.  Table 10 provides an overview of ongoing and planned assistance from the UN system and the Bretton Woods institutions to address HIV/AIDS and other multi-sectoral issues.
HIV/AIDS
ACT NOW.  The UN Country Team has agreed to prepare and implement a joint UN system response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Ukraine.  This joint programme, entitled “ACT NOW”, will support the implementation of the Government’s strategy on HIV/AIDS and improve coordination among Government agencies and between national and international participants. Under ACT NOW, the UN system will assist the Government in the areas of HIV prevention, surveillance, counseling, care and treatment of the disease and in providing institutional support to the concerned Government agencies. UNAIDS will assist the UN Country Team in the overall planning and coordination of ACT NOW, bringing its global experience in addressing HIV/AIDS to the attention of the Government and UN Country Team. Each participating UN agency will plan and manage their components of ACT NOW and will report periodically to the UN Country Team on the status and results of their activities.
The World Bank is negotiating a loan to address HIV/AIDS and tuberculosis in Ukraine that will complement ACT NOW.  
HIV/AIDS Prevention. A large portion of the resources of the UN system dedicated to ACT NOW will focus on prevention of HIV transmission.  Planned interventions for HIV prevention will involve UNAIDS, UNFPA, UNICEF, WHO and ILO.  WHO will address HIV prevention among intravenous drug users as a harm reduction strategy.  UNFPA will support social marketing of condoms and targeted prevention efforts aimed at uniformed services, prisoners and commercial sex workers. UNICEF and UNFPA are working together to develop outreach programmes for youth including “youth friendly clinics”.  UNICEF will support prevention activities for youth particularly those in vulnerable or high-risk groups, prevention of mother to child transmission, and general social mobilization efforts for HIV prevention through mass media.  ILO is planning a project on HIV in the workplace that focuses on prevention and health education activities for workers in the tourism, transport and health care industries.  UNAIDS will provide technical support and advice on prevention activities to UN agencies and the Government.
HIV/AIDS Counseling, Care and Treatment. Under the ACT NOW joint programme, WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, UNDP and ILO will all provide support for activities that enhance counseling, care and treatment for those infected with HIV and AIDS.  WHO will provide technical assistance for improving access to care, improved accessibility of drugs, and voluntary testing and counseling.  UNICEF will support care and treatment for children infected with HIV including the development and implementation of policies and standards for appropriate care for children with HIV.  The “youth friendly” clinics supported by UNICEF and UNFPA will provide health services for young people with HIV and other sexually- transmitted diseases.  UNFPA will also provide capacity building assistance for the various health specializations.  UNDP will address the human rights of people living with HIV/AIDS (PLHAs) and ILO will address the employment rights of PLHAs.
Institutional Support on HIV/AIDS.  UNDP and UNAIDS will provide support for the development of national capacity to plan and manage the implementation of the national strategy on HIV/AIDS.  UNDP will strengthen the capacity of the National secretariat of the National Commission on Prevention of HIV/AIDS, support preparations for a national conference on HIV/AIDS in Ukraine, support follow up activities related to the UN Declaration of Commitment on HIV/AIDS, and support the use of information technology for purposes of networking and information sharing. 
Chernobyl
Development Assistance.  Fifteen years after the Chernobyl nuclear accident, UNDP and UNICEF in cooperation with UNOCHA and other agencies have undertaken a three-country situation analysis of the continuing human consequences of the disaster.  The recommendations of this study have resulted a shift away from humanitarian assistance to a holistic approach to meeting the long-term development needs of the people in the affected area.  UNDP will support employment generation activities for people living in the affected area. UNDP will also provide assistance for social and psychological rehabilitation of the affected population.  UNICEF will support activities in the fields of health and education for children and young people.
Pollution Mitigation.  UNDP will support preventive measures to avert further radioactive pollution of the Dnieper River, the water source for about 30 million people. 
Crimean Re-integration
Conflict Prevention.  The Crimean Integration and Development Programme (CIDP) will continue to provide support for the peaceful re-integration of people who were deported from the Crimea during and after the Second World War.  UNDP and UNHCR have been the lead agencies of the UN system in the CIDP.  UNDP will support development and implementation of an early warning system to gauge the potential for conflict in the Crimean communities where formerly deported people have resettled.  UNDP will also promote peace and tolerance through education system and cultural activities.
Skill Development and Job Creation.  In order to close reduce poverty among returnees, UNDP will support a number of activities to increase their access to resources.  These will include skills training, micro-credit, and business services for entrepreneurs.
Community Development and Infrastructure for Social Services.  In order to improve the quality of life for all residents of communities receiving returnees, UNDP will support strengthening of local government, promotion of broad participation in decision making at the community level, and strengthening of the capacities to provide equal access and to deliver basic social services for education and health.
V.  	Follow Up and Review
Agency Programming.  Agency-specific programming is the logical next step after the UN Country Team has reached consensus on the UNDAF.  However, the timing and duration of agency programme cycles present some problems.  UNDP, UNHCR and UNICEF are at the beginning of their programming cycles, but other agencies, particularly the Bretton Woods institutions are in the midst of theirs.  In addition, most agencies have programming cycles that are shorter than the four-year UNDAF period.  Thus, the UNDAF may serve as a useful starting point for programming for some agencies, but for others, relevant aspects of the UNDAF will need to be incorporated in programme revisions.  All new UN agency programme will be negotiated and agreed between the UN agency and its Government counterpart agency.
Inter-Agency Programming.  The UNDAF has identified opportunities for new or enhanced collaboration that should be considered as agencies prepare and revise their programmes and projects.  Depending on the scope of possible collaboration, these opportunities require further consideration by the UN Country Team as a whole or by a sub-group of the concerned agencies.  The concerned agencies must determine and agree on the appropriate level of inter-agency cooperation (joint planning and implementation of programme activities, coordination of activities by inter-agency consultation or complementary agency-specific activities on different subjects within the same sector or area.)  For any such programming, the concerned UN agencies should prepare programme documentation in a consultative manner that is results-oriented, time-bound and clearly linked to the UNDAF framework.  The programme document should incorporate programme management arrangements to ensure the appropriate degree of inter-agency cooperation and coordination.
Increasing Coordination of UN System Activities during Programme Implementation.  The Resident Coordinator and the UN Country Team will use the UNDAF as a guide to increasing coordination of activities of the UN system during implementation.  In general, the coordination mechanisms are in place; they need to be focussed on coordination of activities.  These coordinating mechanisms include, inter alia, the regular meetings of the UN Country Team, theme groups, working groups, and information sharing arrangements.  The status of the existing theme groups needs to be reviewed and consideration should be given to the desirability of setting up new groups or arrangements corresponding to the five objectives of the UNDAF.
Resource Mobilization and Partnership Development.  The UNDAF and the Common Country Assessment identify areas of need that greatly exceed the resources available to the UN system.  The Resident Coordinator and individual UN agencies should use UNDAF and the CCA in discussions with bi-lateral donors and other potential partners to explain the common policies of the UN system for assistance to Ukraine.  In discussions with potential partners of possible parallel financing, joint programming or cost sharing, the Resident Coordinator and each UN agency should emphasize 1) that the UNDAF has defined common goals for UN assistance in areas of the competencies and mandates of the UN agencies working in Ukraine and the UN Common Country Assessment, 2) that UN agencies have extensive operational experience in Ukraine and strong relationships with Government agencies and civil society organizations; 3)  that UN agency operations are planned and implemented in consultation with Government, development partners and civil society organizations; 4) finally that reporting on these activities by UN agencies is open and transparent.
Monitoring Progress on Millenium Summit Commitments. The UN Resident Coordinator and each UN agency, as appropriate, will use the UNDAF in policy dialogue with the Government, particularly regarding progress towards fulfillment of international commitments of the Government under global conventions and agreements, including meeting reporting obligations.  These commitments were summarized in the Declaration of the Millenium Summit.  While the target dates for achievement of many of the Millenium Summit goals are well beyond the end of the UNDAF period, the UN Country Team should monitor national progress towards achievement of these goals. 
Monitoring and Review of the UNDAF.   Programmes and projects included in the UNDAF and negotiated and agreed with Government will be monitored, reviewed and evaluated by their respective UN sponsors.  These agencies will be responsible for monitoring and evaluation, including the establishment of specific benchmarks and indicators, in accordance with their own procedures.  These UN agency monitoring and evaluation processes will provide the assessment data on the extent to which UNDAF objectives are being achieved.
The UN Resident Coordinator and UN Country Team will review the implementation of the UNDAF regularly at Country Team meetings.  Revisions to the UNDAF, in the form of supplementary memoranda, will be attached to the document when major revisions are made or new programmes are added.  
The Government will be invited periodically to review the implementation of the UNDAF and advise UN system agencies of its findings and recommendations.
Ultimately, the success of the UNDAF will be measured in terms on increased collaboration among UN system agencies and the impact of the contributions of the UN system to the achievement of national goals.
